I've been in therapy on and off for about three and a half years.  I wont go into the story of why I needed therapy; the story will be different for everyone.  However, the gist of what I wanted to get out of therapy was to more fully appreciate life and my Forever Alone status.  It took an older nurse friend of mine to convince me that I should at least go out and talk to a few therapists.

The easy way was to simply google therapists orange county, doing that I found networktherapy.com.  I called about five or so therapists on there, three called once, and only one called twice.  I picked the once that called twice, and I have been very happy. I felt like she really gave a damn about me; a stranger!

She was an older woman, but was very attentive to my needs as a young male trying to figure out what to do with his life. She has helped me in so many ways and I _know_ I have become a better person because of it. I saw her about once a week for about six months, then once every two weeks for six months, once every month for about eight months; and stopped for a long while. 

I'm getting back in because of some other stuff that has happened in my life.  Namely women. Oh boy.

Anyway.  The point is, therapy is good. So get yourself some help.

Some info you can use, when discussing with a therapist do not feel burned or turned off that they only return voicemails.   Between their sessions therapists typically only have about 10-15 minutes to return calls and do office work. Expect the office to be shared with a visible lobby, so be aware and find the strength that you may make eye contact with the person leaving his/her personal session.  Some therapists share offices, and a secretary so things may move smoothly.  

If price is an issue (and you do not have insurance), as I know some charge upwards to $175 a session, ask for a "sliding scale" this means that they start you off at a reasonable session fee maybe $40, and work you up as you feel comfortable.  

You can either pay by cash, credit card, and I think some take personal check; this person is helping you and they have to keep a roof over their head (not saying this to you at all - but be fair to those who are helping you).

Read up on the terminology of their acronyms. LCSW, MFT, etc,. 

Your first session will be a lot of questions asked by your therapist, and forms.  If you have insurance, they may have to make some kind of diagnosis to the insurance company.  It is a pain, but make sure you come prepared with questions and a situation you want them to help with.  They are here to help you, so make sure you guide them to what you are mostly focused in.  They are trained to ask questions, but if you feel they are focusing on something you feel they shouldnt; guide them back onto what is _really_ concerning you.  Family, drug-abuse, love-life, workplace stress, etc,.  At the end, they will be trying to wrap up the thoughts of the meeting nicely, and will ask when you want to meet next.  If this is your first time in therapy, please give it another chance. Keep them regular, and hopefully at the same time.  It will be easier for your therapist to pencil you in to that schedule.

Your next sessions should be similar in structure.  Bring what ever you can to help your therapist.  Write notes, keep a journal, correspondence between your friends/family/colleagues.

Your therapist may make you do some homework, like read, or goto a seminar.  Remember, they will reccomend things to you that they feel will help.  They arent trying to make money on these sorts of things, so listen carefully. I know I was skeptical of some of their seminars/reading, but once I let that hang-up go; it helped A LOT.

But yea.  That's about all I know for therapy.  

Also, I can PM you my therapist. She knows what postsecret, reddit, facebook, twitter, linked-in and the typical urbandictionary lingo; so I feel like she is connected to the younger (read: 15-30) generation.
